topics.title: SQL, data model and data security

questions.question: Give a two-minute overview of NEXUS AI. What does it do and what are its main parts?
questions.answer: NEXUS AI is a multi-tenant enterprise assistant with two user-facing capabilities: grounded document Q&A with citations (POST /api/v1/chat/ask) and a multi-agent 'customer purchase-decline investigation' that reads ERP/CRM/email data plus indexed documents, writes a report that separates evidence from hypotheses, and drafts follow-up emails that only go out after a manager approves them. The backend is FastAPI + SQLAlchemy on PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector; ingestion runs through a Postgres-backed job queue; orchestration uses a LangGraph StateGraph whose nodes are wrapped in a checkpointing runtime; tools live in a typed registry that is also exposed over MCP. The frontend is React 19 + Vite served by nginx. It runs keyless by default with a deterministic local LLM adapter and a hashing embedder, and can switch to Gemini or OpenAI via settings.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers want a crisp, layered summary (user value -> components -> key engineering choices), not a file listing. A strong answer also volunteers what is NOT real (local adapter, synthetic connectors).
follow_ups: Which part was hardest to build and why?
What would you cut if you had one week?
Who is the target user?

questions.question: Why does the project ship a deterministic 'local' LLM provider instead of requiring an API key?
questions.answer: LocalProvider in llm/local.py implements each task (answer_question, plan_workflow, analyze_evidence, draft_email) with transparent rule-based heuristics over the structured payload, so the whole system - tests, CI, e2e, demos - runs without secrets or cost and produces reproducible output. It is always reported as provider='local', model='rule-based-v1', with tokens_are_estimates=True, and the UI shows a 'Deterministic local adapter' badge so nobody mistakes it for a real model. ADR-001 records the decision. The trade-off is that answer quality and hypothesis detection are keyword-level only; the Gemini/OpenAI adapters exist but are not exercised in CI.
questions.reasoning: Probes honesty about AI capability and testability. The pitfall is presenting a rule engine as 'AI'; the strong answer explains how the provider boundary keeps the rest of the code identical.
follow_ups: How would you know the real provider behaves like the local one?
What breaks if a real model returns different JSON?

questions.question: Walk through the main database tables and what each group is for.
questions.answer: Identity: organizations and users (role in admin/manager/analyst/viewer). Knowledge: documents, chunks (text, 384-dim pgvector embedding, generated tsvector, flags) and ingestion_jobs. Chat: conversations, messages (with citations JSONB) and memory_items (explicit user preferences, unique per user+key). Workflows: workflow_runs (status, plan, checkpointed state JSONB, token budget), workflow_steps (unique per run+name, output, tool_calls), approval_requests and outbox_messages (both with unique idempotency_key), audit_events and usage_records. Business demo data: crm_customers, erp_orders, erp_quotations, email_records. Every tenant-owned table carries an indexed org_id.
questions.reasoning: Checks whether the candidate understands their own data model and can relate tables to features and invariants (uniqueness, cascade).
follow_ups: Why is org_id duplicated on chunks when documents already has it?
Which constraints enforce idempotency?

questions.question: What is real and what is simulated in this project? Be precise.
questions.answer: Real: the API, auth (argon2 + JWT), Postgres/pgvector schema and migrations, ingestion pipeline (validation, extraction for PDF/DOCX/XLSX/CSV/MD/TXT/HTML, chunking, injection scanning, embedding, indexing), hybrid retrieval with RRF and a lexical reranker, LangGraph orchestration with checkpoints, the tool registry, approvals, idempotency, audit, MCP server, React UI and tests. Simulated: the LLM by default (rule-based LocalProvider), embeddings by default (feature hashing, lexical not semantic), the business systems (seeded CRM/ERP/email tables behind connectors/business.py) and email sending (an outbox table, no SMTP). Gemini/OpenAI adapters are written against SDK signatures but untested live, and nothing has been deployed to the cloud.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers test integrity. Overclaiming is the most common failure in portfolio interviews.
follow_ups: How would you replace the outbox with a real email provider?
How do you demonstrate value without a real LLM?

questions.question: What measured numbers can you quote about the system, and what do they actually mean?
questions.answer: Tests: 85 backend pytest tests against a real Postgres + pgvector database, 4 vitest component tests and 4 Playwright e2e tests. Latency from scripts/benchmark_latency.py, written to docs/benchmarks/latency.json: chat ask p50 37.9 ms / p95 52.1 ms over 30 calls, and a full investigation about 1.33 s p50 over 3 runs. These were in-process service calls with the local LLM and local embedder on a Windows dev machine with Postgres in Docker, so they measure retrieval + DB + orchestration overhead only. With a remote model, per-call model latency (seconds) dominates and the numbers do not transfer. No accuracy percentages are claimed; quality evaluation lives in the separate EvalOps project.
questions.reasoning: Probes whether the candidate understands the conditions of a benchmark and avoids quoting numbers out of context.
follow_ups: How would you benchmark with a real provider?
Why p95 and not max for chat?

questions.question: Which user roles exist and what can each do?
questions.answer: ROLES are viewer, analyst, manager and admin, ranked 0-3 in ROLE_RANK. Viewers can ask questions (chat/ask requires 'viewer'). Analysts can upload documents, ingest URLs, start and resume investigations and call most tools (default tool min_role). Managers can decide approvals (APPROVER_MIN_ROLE), delete documents, and read audit, usage and outbox admin endpoints. Admins additionally list users. The same ranks are enforced in FastAPI dependencies (require_role) and inside the tool registry, and the frontend hides controls with hasRole, which is UX only.
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding of layered authorization and that UI gating is not security.
follow_ups: Why rank-based instead of permission sets?
How would you add a custom role like 'auditor'?

questions.question: How are settings loaded and validated, and what protects production from a weak JWT secret?
questions.answer: core/config.py defines a pydantic-settings Settings class reading env vars and .env files, with Literal types for enums like llm_provider and ingestion_mode. A field validator rewrites postgresql:// URLs to the psycopg driver. A model_validator (_production_safety) refuses to start when APP_ENV=production and the JWT secret contains 'change-me'/'insecure' or is shorter than 32 chars, and refuses provider=gemini/openai without the matching API key. get_settings is lru_cached so it is parsed once.
questions.reasoning: Fail-fast configuration is a classic production-readiness signal. Pitfall: lru_cache means tests must call cache_clear (conftest does).
follow_ups: What else would you validate at startup?
How do you change settings in tests given the cache?

questions.question: How does error handling produce a consistent JSON envelope?
questions.answer: core/errors.py defines AppError with status_code and code, and subclasses NotFound(404), Forbidden(403), Unauthorized(401), Conflict(409) and RateLimited(429); domain errors like UploadRejected (415) and UnsafeUrl (400) subclass it too. install_error_handlers registers handlers for AppError, RequestValidationError (422 with loc/msg details) and a catch-all Exception that logs only the error type and returns a generic 500. Every envelope includes the request_id from request.state so a user-reported error can be correlated with logs and audit rows.
questions.reasoning: Probes API design discipline and avoiding leaking stack traces. Follow-up often asks about mapping errors in background tasks, which have no request.
follow_ups: Why not return exception messages for 500s?
How does the frontend use the code field?

questions.question: Explain the request-context middleware in main.py. Why validate the incoming X-Request-ID?
questions.answer: The http middleware accepts an incoming X-Request-ID only if, after removing dashes, it is alphanumeric and at most 64 chars; otherwise it generates uuid4().hex. It stores the id on request.state and in a ContextVar (request_id_var) so the audit service can stamp audit_events.request_id without passing it through every function. It sets security headers (nosniff, X-Frame-Options DENY, Referrer-Policy no-referrer), echoes X-Request-ID, and logs method/path/status/ms. Validation prevents log injection and unbounded values from untrusted clients; nginx sets X-Request-ID from $request_id so the id spans proxy and API.
questions.reasoning: Tests observability fundamentals and awareness that every header is attacker-controlled.
follow_ups: Why a ContextVar rather than a thread-local?
How would this propagate into background tasks?

questions.question: How are database sessions managed in request handlers versus background work?
questions.answer: core/db.py lazily creates one Engine (pool_pre_ping, pool_size=10) and a sessionmaker with expire_on_commit=False. Request handlers get a session via the get_db generator dependency, which always closes it. Background code (execute_run, run_step, the worker, the MCP handler) never reuses a request session; each opens its own with session_factory()() in a with-block. run_step even opens a fresh session per attempt and _execute uses its own session in the pool thread, because SQLAlchemy sessions are not thread-safe.
questions.reasoning: Session-per-unit-of-work and thread confinement are frequent sources of production bugs; interviewers look for that awareness.
follow_ups: What does expire_on_commit=False buy you and what does it risk?
What happens with pool_size=10 and 8 step threads plus requests?

questions.question: Why are most route handlers plain 'def' rather than 'async def'?
questions.answer: The handlers call synchronous SQLAlchemy (psycopg) and CPU-bound code like embedding or argon2. FastAPI runs sync 'def' endpoints in its threadpool, so blocking calls do not stall the event loop. The upload endpoint is async because it awaits UploadFile.read with a bounded size, then calls the sync _store helper - which does block the loop briefly while it hashes, validates and writes the file.
questions.reasoning: Distinguishes candidates who understand the event loop from those who sprinkle async everywhere.
follow_ups: When would you switch to async SQLAlchemy?
What is the default threadpool size and why does it matter?

questions.question: How is structured logging configured, and how are secrets kept out of logs?
questions.answer: configure_logging sets structlog with merge_contextvars, log level, ISO timestamps, a custom _redact processor and JSON rendering. _redact replaces values of keys containing password/secret/token/api_key/authorization with [REDACTED] and regex-masks secret-like 'key=value' patterns inside string values. Code also avoids logging prompts or bodies: errors log error_type, not messages with content. Regex redaction is a safety net, not a guarantee, so the primary control is not logging sensitive fields at all.
questions.reasoning: Probes data-handling hygiene. A good answer distinguishes defense-in-depth redaction from the policy of not logging payloads.
follow_ups: What PII might still leak?
How would you ship these logs to CloudWatch?

questions.question: What does the lifespan handler do at startup and shutdown, and what multi-replica bug did it have?
questions.answer: On startup it configures logging and calls mark_interrupted_runs; failure is logged but does not block boot (readiness reports the DB). If INGESTION_MODE=embedded it starts a daemon thread running _embedded_worker, which polls claim_next/run_job; on shutdown it sets a threading.Event to stop that loop. The original mark_interrupted_runs flipped EVERY 'running' run to 'interrupted', which is wrong with several API replicas: a rolling restart of one replica would break runs executing on a healthy one. It was found in code review and fixed: a run is only marked interrupted when its latest step activity (max of step finished_at/started_at, else created_at) is older than stale_after_seconds() = step timeout x max attempts + 60 s, i.e. longer than any live step could stay silent. test_startup_recovery_only_marks_stale_runs covers both the fresh and the stale case.
questions.reasoning: Probes crash-recovery assumptions in multi-replica deployments, and whether the candidate can explain a bug they found and fixed.
follow_ups: Why is an activity-based heuristic weaker than an explicit owner lease?
What happens if a single step legitimately runs longer than the threshold?

questions.question: How is the upload size limit enforced without reading an unbounded body into memory?
questions.answer: The upload route reads at most limit+1 bytes with await file.read(limit + 1), and rejects with 413 if more came back; validate_upload re-checks the size. The filename is normalized (backslashes to slashes, basename only, max 200 chars) before use, and the title is capped at 300 chars. nginx also caps the request body at 16m (client_max_body_size), slightly above the 15 MB default MAX_UPLOAD_MB. Note that Starlette may already have spooled the multipart file to a temp file; the bounded read limits what the app buffers in memory.
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding of DoS vectors around uploads and layered limits.
follow_ups: Where else can request size be limited?
What about URL ingestion size?

questions.question: Describe the layering of the backend code.
questions.answer: api/* are thin FastAPI routers: parse input with Pydantic schemas, resolve the user via dependencies, call a service, map to an output model. services/* hold business logic (chat, retrieval, workflows, approvals, audit). agents/* contain the LangGraph graph and the checkpointing runtime. tools/* is the typed registry plus built-in tools; connectors/business.py is the only code that queries the CRM/ERP/email tables. ingestion/* is the document pipeline; llm/* hides providers behind a Protocol; core/* has config, db, security, errors, logging, rate limiting; models/* are SQLAlchemy ORM classes. Dependencies point inward: routers -> services -> tools/connectors/llm -> models.
questions.reasoning: Checks the candidate can explain separation of concerns and where a new feature would go.
follow_ups: Where would you add a Salesforce connector?
Is there any place where the layering is violated?

questions.question: How does the LLM provider abstraction work and how is a provider chosen?
questions.answer: llm/base.py defines LLMRequest (task, system, user, payload, tier fast|strong), a Usage dataclass and an LLMProvider Protocol with generate(request, schema) -> (validated Pydantic object, Usage). get_llm() in llm/__init__.py is lru_cached and returns GeminiProvider, OpenAIProvider or LocalProvider based on settings.llm_provider. Real providers use system/user prompts; the local adapter uses the structured payload. Because callers only see a typed object, swapping providers does not change services or agents.
questions.reasoning: Tests interface design and the trick of sending both a prompt and a structured payload.
follow_ups: Why a Protocol and not an ABC?
How would you add Anthropic or a self-hosted model?

questions.question: How does the embedded ingestion worker differ from the separate worker process, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: INGESTION_MODE=embedded (default) makes the API's lifespan start a daemon thread that loops claim_next/run_job; it is convenient for local dev because a single process handles everything. INGESTION_MODE=worker leaves the API free and expects `python -m app.worker` (same image) to poll the job table; docker-compose sets api to worker mode and runs a separate worker service. The worker handles SIGINT/SIGTERM by finishing the current loop iteration. Because claiming uses SKIP LOCKED, N worker replicas can run safely. Production should use worker mode so CPU-heavy extraction and embedding do not compete with request handling.
questions.reasoning: Probes deployment topology thinking and the reason the same code supports both modes.
follow_ups: What happens to an in-flight job when the worker gets SIGTERM?
How would you autoscale workers?

questions.question: Why is the investigation started with FastAPI BackgroundTasks, and what are the consequences?
questions.answer: POST /workflows creates the run (status running) synchronously, returns 202 with the run, and schedules wf.execute_run(run.id) via BackgroundTasks, which runs after the response in the API process. That is simple and keeps state in Postgres so the UI polls GET /workflows/{id}. Consequences: execution is bound to the API process lifetime (a crash leaves the run 'running' until startup recovery marks it interrupted), there is no global concurrency limit or queue, and long runs occupy threadpool threads. A production version would enqueue runs into a durable queue (a workflow_jobs table like ingestion_jobs, or a broker) consumed by workers.
questions.reasoning: Classic challenge: did you choose the simplest thing knowingly, and can you name the failure modes?
follow_ups: How would you cap concurrent runs per tenant?
How does TestClient handle background tasks in tests?

questions.question: How is the frontend structured and how does it talk to the API?
questions.answer: React 19 + react-router with pages for Login, Chat, Documents, Investigations, RunDetail, Approvals and Admin. api/client.ts is a small typed fetch wrapper that prefixes /api/v1, attaches the bearer token from sessionStorage, sets JSON content type, maps error envelopes to an ApiError(status, code, message, requestId) and clears the token on 401. AuthProvider loads /auth/me on start. Long-running state is polled: Documents reloads every 1.5 s while ingestion is pending and RunDetail every 1.2 s while a run is active. In production nginx serves the static build and proxies /api/ to the API, so the browser is same-origin.
questions.reasoning: Tests full-stack understanding and why same-origin proxying simplifies CORS and CSP.
follow_ups: Why polling instead of SSE/WebSockets?
What would you change to support streaming answers?

questions.question: Where is state stored for an investigation run, and why are there two notions of state?
questions.answer: In memory, LangGraph carries InvestigationState (plan, top_customers, declining, research, analysis, report, approvals) between nodes. Durably, run_step writes each step's output and tool_calls into workflow_steps and merges the output dict into workflow_runs.state (the checkpoint), and run.tokens_used is incremented. On resume, execute_run seeds the graph with run.state and run_step returns the stored output for completed steps. ADR-004 calls this out: two states must be kept in sync by run_step, in exchange for queryable, UI-friendly step records instead of LangGraph's opaque serialized checkpoints.
questions.reasoning: Probes understanding of checkpoint semantics and the cost of a custom design.
follow_ups: What if a step's output is not JSON-serializable?
What if two steps write the same state key?

questions.question: Why is every side effect funneled through the approvals service?
questions.answer: ADR-005: agents may only draft. The draft_followup_email tool creates an ApprovalRequest (status pending) and never sends. send_email is registered with requires_approval=True, min_role manager, side_effect external and mcp_exposed=False, and the registry refuses it unless ToolContext.approved_action_id is set - which only services/approvals.approve does, after checking the user is manager+ and the request is pending under a row lock. That gives one auditable choke point for anything that leaves the system.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers test human-in-the-loop design and whether the guard is structural rather than prompt-based.
follow_ups: Could a prompt-injected agent bypass this?
How would you add a second side-effect type like 'create CRM task'?

questions.question: Why are business data access functions in connectors/business.py rather than inside tools?
questions.answer: The connectors module is the seam between NEXUS and systems of record. Each function (search_customers, top_customers_with_trend, customer_orders, pending_quotations, search_emails) takes db and org_id explicitly and returns plain dicts, so a production deployment could implement the same signatures against Salesforce, SAP or Gmail APIs. Tools stay focused on validation, permission and shape; connectors own querying and tenant scoping. as_of_date anchors analysis to the latest order date so demo results are reproducible.
questions.reasoning: Probes adapter/port thinking and testability.
follow_ups: How would you handle pagination and rate limits of a real CRM API?
How would you cache connector results?

questions.question: Design question: how would you scale this architecture to many tenants and ~10M chunks?
questions.answer: Retrieval: keep pgvector but partition chunks (e.g. by org_id hash or list partitions for big tenants) so HNSW indexes stay small and filtered searches do not post-filter a global index; for very large tenants consider a dedicated vector store. Tune hnsw ef_search and use pgvector iterative scans for filtered queries, and move to real semantic embeddings (re-index required). Ingestion: run N workers, add heartbeats so long jobs are not reclaimed at 10 min, and batch embedding calls with retries and backoff. Workflows: move execution out of API BackgroundTasks into a durable run queue with per-tenant concurrency limits. Infra: read replicas for retrieval, PgBouncer, Redis rate limiting, S3 for objects, OTel tracing. None of this is implemented today; the current single-database design is sized for a demo.
questions.reasoning: Senior system design. Looks for bottleneck identification (filtered ANN, worker throughput, run execution) rather than buzzwords.
follow_ups: Where is the first bottleneck you would hit?
How do you re-embed 10M chunks without downtime?

questions.question: How would you add a second agent workflow type (for example a quotation follow-up sweep)?
questions.answer: Today WorkflowRun.kind is hard-coded 'investigation', build_graph builds one graph, and the planner only emits customer_decline_investigation or unsupported. I would: add a new intent to WorkflowPlan, create agents/quotation.py with its own state TypedDict, agent functions and a build_graph; keep wrapping every node with run_step so checkpoints, retries, budgets and audit come for free; register any new tools in the registry with min_role and side_effect; route side effects through draft tools + approvals; set run.kind from the plan and dispatch in execute_run on kind; and add integration tests with failure injection like the existing ones. The roadmap lists more workflow types as future work - not implemented.
questions.reasoning: Probes extensibility and whether the candidate reuses the runtime guarantees instead of re-implementing them.
follow_ups: How would the supervisor choose between graphs?
How would you version graphs so old runs can still resume?

questions.question: What structured output schemas does the system request from LLMs?
questions.answer: schemas/llm_outputs.py defines GroundedAnswer (answer, cited_context_ids, insufficient_evidence), WorkflowPlan (intent Literal, steps as a list of a Literal AgentName, top_n 1-50, lookback_months 1-24, rationale), Evidence (statement, source), Hypothesis (statement, confidence low|medium|high, supporting_sources), CustomerFinding, EvidenceAnalysis (summary + findings) and EmailDraft (subject max 200, body max 4000). Literals and bounds make invalid plans impossible to represent after validation.

Which fields would a model most often get wrong?

questions.question: How do the remote providers enforce structured output and handle invalid JSON?
questions.answer: GeminiProvider passes response_mime_type='application/json' and response_json_schema=schema.model_json_schema(); OpenAIProvider uses response_format type json_schema with the Pydantic schema. Both use temperature 0.2, then validate with schema.model_validate_json. On ValidationError (or JSONDecodeError for OpenAI) they do exactly one repair retry, feeding back a truncated error message - Gemini appends it to the user prompt, OpenAI appends the bad assistant reply plus a correction message. After two failures they raise StructuredOutputError. Usage is recorded from provider token counts and costed via PRICE_TABLE.
questions.reasoning: Probes practical robustness patterns for LLM JSON. Pitfall: trusting provider-side schema enforcement without validating locally.
follow_ups: Is the usage of the failed first attempt recorded?
When would you not retry at all?

questions.question: How does the local answerer decide whether to answer or abstain?
questions.answer: _answer tokenizes the question (stopwords removed, crude suffix stripping), splits each context into sentences and scores sentences by query-term coverage plus a small overlap/length bonus minus a position penalty. If no sentence covers at least 60% of the question's content terms it returns insufficient_evidence=True. Otherwise it takes up to three distinct sentences scoring at least 75% of the best and builds an extractive answer with [id] markers. The threshold exists because an earlier version answered 'What is the capital of France?' from 'capital expenditure'; there is a regression test for abstention.
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding of grounded abstention and that thresholds were driven by observed bugs.
follow_ups: How would you calibrate the threshold with a real model?
What does the e2e test check about abstention?

questions.question: What does validate_citations do and what does it not guarantee?
questions.answer: After generation, validate_citations keeps only cited_context_ids within 1..n_contexts, extracts [n] markers from the answer text, strips markers that point to nonexistent contexts, unions the valid ids, and forces insufficient_evidence=True when no valid citation remains. The chat service then builds citation objects (document, page, section, 400-char snippet, flagged) only from those ids. It guarantees that citations reference contexts that were actually retrieved; it does not verify that the cited text supports the claim. Entailment or groundedness checks are left to evaluation (EvalOps) or a future judge step.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers want the distinction between referential integrity of citations and factual faithfulness.
follow_ups: How would you add a faithfulness check cheaply?
Should an answer with zero citations be shown at all?

questions.question: ground_sources filters the analysis agent's sources. What is its weakness?
questions.answer: ground_sources builds, per customer, the set of source ids actually gathered (erp_orders, erp_quotations:<n>, email:<id>, document:<id>#p<page>), drops findings for unknown customers (hallucinated customer), removes evidence items whose source is not in the set and removes unknown supporting_sources from hypotheses. Weakness: it validates the source labels, not the statements. A model could attach a real email id to an invented quote or number and it would pass. Also a hypothesis whose sources are all removed is kept with an empty list (rendered as 'supported by: none') rather than dropped or downgraded. Stronger checks: require evidence statements to be verbatim substrings of the source text, recompute numbers from ERP data, and drop unsupported hypotheses.
questions.reasoning: A deliberate challenge question: can the candidate see the limits of their own guardrail?
follow_ups: Implement the verbatim-quote check.
Should numeric claims ever come from the model?

questions.question: How does the supervisor's plan get sanitized before it drives the graph?
questions.answer: The supervisor calls ctx.llm with task plan_workflow and schema WorkflowPlan, so steps must already be valid AgentName literals and top_n/lookback_months are bounded. It then reorders and filters the steps with [s for s in AGENT_ORDER if s in plan.steps], enforcing the canonical order and discarding duplicates. The conditional router only moves forward through AGENT_ORDER, so the model cannot create loops. If intent is 'unsupported', execute_run marks the run failed with the planner's rationale.
questions.reasoning: Tests the idea of constraining model decisions with code (allow-lists and ordering) rather than trusting the plan.
follow_ups: What if the plan skips data_agent but keeps analysis_agent?
Would you ever let the model choose arbitrary tools?

questions.question: How would you safely switch production from the local adapter to a real LLM?
questions.answer: Steps: set LLM_PROVIDER and keys (settings already refuse a provider without its key); run the EvalOps golden set against the chat contract with both providers and compare citation precision/recall, abstention correctness and latency; run the investigation integration tests against the real model in a non-CI job since outputs are nondeterministic; keep all code-side guards (schema validation, validate_citations, ground_sources, approvals, budgets) unchanged. Watch token budgets (60k default) and per-step timeouts (30 s) because real calls are slower, add provider timeouts/retries, egress through an allowlisting proxy, and ship behind a per-tenant flag with usage_records monitoring cost. Also switch embeddings deliberately: EMBEDDING_PROVIDER change requires full re-index.
questions.reasoning: Senior question about change management for AI systems, evaluation gates and rollout.
follow_ups: What metric would block the rollout?
How do you handle provider outages?

questions.question: What is hybrid retrieval and how is it implemented here?
questions.answer: hybrid_search runs two candidate queries over the same tenant-scoped base query (chunks joined to ready documents of the user's org): a pgvector cosine-distance ordering on chunk embeddings and a Postgres full-text search on the generated tsvector column ranked by ts_rank_cd, each limited to 25 candidates. The two ranked lists are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (score += 1/(60 + rank)), then a lexical reranker reorders and the top k (6 for chat) are returned. Hybrid helps because vectors catch paraphrase (with a semantic embedder) while full-text catches exact identifiers and rare terms.
questions.reasoning: Basic RAG literacy plus specifics of this implementation.
follow_ups: Why fuse by rank rather than by score?
Why 25 candidates per side?

questions.question: Explain Reciprocal Rank Fusion and why k=60.
questions.answer: RRF assigns each document sum over lists of 1/(k + rank). It needs only ranks, so it combines cosine distances and ts_rank_cd scores that live on incomparable scales without normalization. k dampens the advantage of top ranks: with k=60 the difference between rank 1 and rank 5 is small, so a document ranked moderately in both lists can beat one ranked first in only one list. 60 is the value from the original RRF paper and a common default; RRF_K is a module constant here. Chunks found by only one retriever get a single term.
questions.reasoning: Tests whether the candidate can derive the formula and reason about the constant, not just name-drop RRF.
follow_ups: What happens with k=1?
How would you weight one retriever more than the other?

questions.question: How does the reranker work and why is it there?
questions.answer: rerank computes for each candidate: coverage = share of query terms present in chunk text + document title, bigram = share of query bigrams present, and rrf_norm = rrf_score / max rrf. The final score is 0.5*coverage + 0.2*bigram + 0.3*rrf_norm, and the signals are returned in the API 'retrieval' field for debugging. It is local and deterministic, and rewards chunks that cover more of the question, which pairs well with the lexical hashing embedder. A cross-encoder or LLM reranker is the documented upgrade behind the same function.
questions.reasoning: Probes understanding of two-stage retrieval and explainability of ranking.
follow_ups: Why include the document title in coverage?
What are the risks of hand-tuned weights?

questions.question: How are documents chunked, and how is page/section metadata preserved?
questions.answer: Extractors return Segments with page and section: PDFs one per page, DOCX split at Heading-styled paragraphs (tables appended), XLSX one per sheet with 'header: value' rows, CSV as 'header: value' rows, Markdown split at headings. chunk_segments splits each segment at sentence boundaries or blank lines, packs pieces up to 900 chars, carries ~150 chars of overlap (trimmed to a word boundary), hard-splits pieces longer than 900 chars, and never crosses segment boundaries, so every chunk has one page and section. _mk prefixes '[section]' to the chunk text so section headings are searchable and estimates tokens at ~4 chars/token.
questions.reasoning: Chunking quality drives RAG quality; interviewers want concrete parameters and reasons.
follow_ups: Why character-based rather than token-based sizes?
Why not let chunks span pages?

questions.question: What are the weaknesses of the hashing embedder?
questions.answer: HashingEmbedder maps unigrams and bigrams (after stopword removal and crude suffix stripping) into 384 dims with blake2b-derived index and sign, then L2-normalizes. It is deterministic and keyless, but purely lexical: synonyms and paraphrases ('cheaper' vs 'lower price') get no similarity, so the 'vector' leg mostly duplicates the full-text leg. Hash collisions add noise, there is no IDF weighting so frequent words dominate, the suffix stripper is naive, and it is English-only. The fix is EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=gemini/openai (both produce 384-dim vectors to fit the column), which requires re-indexing every chunk.
questions.reasoning: A standard challenge: does the candidate know their 'semantic search' is not semantic by default?
follow_ups: How would you detect a mixed index after switching embedders?
Would TF-IDF weighting help?

questions.question: How is the full-text query built, and is it safe against tsquery syntax injection?
questions.answer: _ts_query lowercases the query, extracts [a-z0-9]+ tokens longer than 2 chars, dedupes and sorts them, keeps the first 30 and joins with ' | ' (OR) for recall, leaving precision to ranking. Because tokens are restricted to [a-z0-9], user input cannot inject tsquery operators like ! & : or parentheses into to_tsquery. Two subtle effects: alphabetical sorting before truncation means long queries drop terms arbitrarily (later-alphabet words), and terms of 2 chars or fewer are dropped, so a code like 'MC-5521' is searched only as '5521'.
questions.reasoning: Probes security of query construction and attention to subtle behaviour in one's own code.
follow_ups: Why not use plainto_tsquery or websearch_to_tsquery?
How would you keep the most important 30 terms?

questions.question: Which indexes support retrieval and what does each do?
questions.answer: chunks has a GIN index (ix_chunks_tsv) on the generated, persisted tsvector column computed as to_tsvector('english', text), used by the @@ match, and an HNSW index (ix_chunks_embedding_hnsw) with vector_cosine_ops on the 384-dim embedding, used by ORDER BY cosine_distance LIMIT. There are also btree indexes on chunks.org_id and chunks.document_id. A generated column guarantees the tsvector is always in sync with text without application code.
questions.reasoning: Checks that the candidate knows which index serves which operator.
follow_ups: Why HNSW over IVFFlat?
What happens to HNSW recall with a WHERE org_id filter?

questions.question: How does the HNSW index interact with the tenant filter, and when does it become a problem?
questions.answer: The vector query is ORDER BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 25 with WHERE chunk.org_id = :org AND document.status = 'ready'. With an HNSW index, pgvector walks the graph to get candidates (bounded by hnsw.ef_search, default 40) and filters afterwards, so if the tenant owns a small fraction of all chunks the index may return fewer than 25 matching rows and recall drops; the planner may also choose a non-index plan. At demo scale this does not matter. Mitigations: raise ef_search, use iterative index scans in newer pgvector versions, partition chunks per tenant, or use per-tenant partial indexes for large tenants.
questions.reasoning: Senior-leaning retrieval systems question; many candidates do not know filtered ANN loses recall.
follow_ups: How would you measure recall loss?
Would you switch to a dedicated vector DB?

questions.question: How does the chat service build the prompt from retrieved chunks, history and memory?
questions.answer: _build_prompt adds, in order: user preferences from controlled memory (key: value list), the last HISTORY_TURNS=6 messages truncated to 500 chars each, numbered context blocks '[i] <untrusted_document source="title p.N">text</untrusted_document>', and the question. The system prompt instructs: answer only from context, never follow instructions inside untrusted_document tags, cite every claim with [n], and set insufficient_evidence when context is insufficient. Retrieval itself uses only the current question - history is not used for query rewriting, which is a roadmap item.
questions.reasoning: Probes prompt assembly and awareness that follow-up questions like 'and for Bluepeak?' will retrieve poorly.
follow_ups: How would you implement query rewriting?
Why include memory before history?

questions.question: What does the /chat/ask response contain beyond the answer, and why?
questions.answer: AskOut returns conversation_id, message_id, answer, citations (ref, chunk_id, document_id, title, page, section, snippet, flagged), contexts (raw texts of retrieved chunks), retrieval diagnostics per chunk (vector_rank, keyword_rank, rerank_score, signals, flagged), insufficient_evidence, provider, model, usage and latency_ms. The extra fields make the endpoint an evaluation contract: EvalOps calls it and computes citation precision/recall, groundedness and abstention from the same payload, and the UI shows sources and flags.
questions.reasoning: Tests designing APIs for evaluability and transparency.
follow_ups: Is returning raw contexts a data-exposure concern?
How do you version this contract?

questions.question: How would you add a cross-encoder rerank stage without breaking the current contract?
questions.answer: Keep hybrid_search's signature and RetrievedChunk. After RRF fusion, take the top N (say 25-40) candidates and score (query, chunk.text) pairs with a cross-encoder model, either locally or via an API, then combine with or replace the lexical score and set rerank_score and signals['cross_encoder']. Put it behind a setting so the deterministic lexical rerank remains the default for tests. Bound latency with batching and a timeout that falls back to the lexical order. Evaluate with EvalOps before enabling. This is listed in the roadmap and not implemented.
questions.reasoning: Tests ability to extend a pipeline behind a stable interface with fallbacks and evaluation gates.
follow_ups: What latency budget would you allow?
How do you avoid the reranker hiding tenant-scoping bugs?

questions.question: How would you re-embed the whole corpus when switching embedding providers, without downtime or a mixed index?
questions.answer: Today indexer.py records the embedder name in document.meta['embedder'], but hybrid_search does not check it, and the column is fixed at Vector(384), so switching EMBEDDING_PROVIDER silently mixes vector spaces until every document is re-indexed. A safe migration: add an embedding_model column (or a second vector column / shadow table), backfill new embeddings in batches via the job queue, build the HNSW index on the new column, switch queries with a flag once coverage is 100% (filtering by model during transition), then drop the old column. For different dimensions a new column is required anyway. Validate with an eval run before cutover.
questions.reasoning: Senior data-migration thinking for vector stores; looks for awareness that vectors from different models are not comparable.
follow_ups: How long would 10M chunks take and cost?
How do you roll back?

questions.question: What agents make up the investigation and what does each one do?
questions.answer: supervisor plans (which agents, top_n, lookback months). data_agent calls get_top_customers and, for customers whose change_pct is -10% or worse, get_customer_orders for monthly history. research_agent gathers per declining customer up to 4 inbound emails, pending quotations and up to 3 customer-specific document excerpts. analysis_agent asks the model (strong tier) to separate evidence from hypotheses, then ground_sources filters sources. report_agent assembles sections and calls generate_report. action_agent drafts one email per finding via the model and calls draft_followup_email, which creates pending approvals.
questions.reasoning: Basic understanding of the multi-agent decomposition and where the model is actually used (3 kinds of calls).
follow_ups: Why is data_agent deterministic with no LLM call?
How many model calls does a run make?

questions.question: How does the LangGraph graph route between agents?
questions.answer: build_graph creates a StateGraph(InvestigationState) with nodes supervisor plus the five agents, each wrapped so it executes through run_step(run_id, seq, name, agent, fn, state). START -> supervisor, then every node has conditional edges via route_from(current): it looks at state['plan']['steps'] and returns the next agent in AGENT_ORDER after the current one that appears in the plan, else END. So the plan can skip agents but never reorder or loop.
questions.reasoning: Checks that the candidate knows how conditional edges are used and the deliberate restriction to forward-only routing.
follow_ups: How would you support a loop like 'research more if evidence is thin'?
Why compile the graph per run?

questions.question: Walk through run_step: how are checkpoints, retries and timeouts implemented?
questions.answer: run_step first looks up workflow_steps by (run_id, name): if completed it returns the stored output (checkpoint hit); otherwise it creates the step row. For each attempt up to WORKFLOW_STEP_MAX_ATTEMPTS (3) it marks the step running, submits _execute to a ThreadPoolExecutor (8 workers) and waits fut.result(timeout=WORKFLOW_STEP_TIMEOUT_S, default 30). _execute runs the agent with its own session and, on success, writes step output, tool_calls, increments run.tokens_used and merges output into run.state in one commit. Timeouts and generic exceptions are retryable with exponential backoff (0.25 s doubling, capped at 2 s); BudgetExceeded, ToolError, Forbidden, AppError and ValueError are not. Final failure raises StepFailed (budget flag set for budget errors).
questions.reasoning: Core of the agent runtime; interviewers check precise understanding of retry classification and atomic checkpoint commit.
follow_ups: Why is ValueError non-retryable?
What if the process dies between step commit and the next step?

questions.question: A timed-out step thread cannot be killed in Python. How does the runtime cope, and what can still go wrong?
questions.answer: On timeout run_step sets a threading.Event (cancelled) and moves on to retry. The orphaned _execute thread keeps running until fn returns; it then checks cancelled and rolls back its session, so none of its DB writes (step completion, state merge, usage records, approval rows created via flush) are committed. What can still go wrong: the zombie consumes a pool slot and real model tokens that are never recorded in usage_records; the retry may run concurrently with the zombie; any non-transactional side effect (an HTTP call to a real provider or connector) has already happened; and the cancel check only happens at the end. ADR-004 acknowledges this. Cooperative cancellation checks inside StepContext.tool/llm, or running steps in a separate process, would be stronger.
questions.reasoning: Deliberate challenge about thread semantics and side effects; distinguishes senior engineers.
follow_ups: How would you add cooperative cancellation?
Why might the 8-thread pool become exhausted?

questions.question: Why build your own checkpoints instead of using LangGraph's Postgres checkpointer?
questions.answer: ADR-004: LangGraph's checkpointer stores serialized graph state that is opaque to SQL and the UI. The project wanted relational, queryable step rows (status, attempts, timestamps, tool_calls, error) that directly power the agent-activity UI, the audit trail and resume-from-first-incomplete-step, plus per-step timeouts, retry classification and budget enforcement in one place. The costs: two notions of state to keep consistent, step identity by name (renaming a node breaks resume of old runs), no time-travel/forking, and outputs must be JSON-serializable. With LangGraph's checkpointer you would still need a separate business-level audit trail.
questions.reasoning: Challenge question probing whether the choice was deliberate and what was given up.
follow_ups: When would you switch to the built-in checkpointer?
How would you support human-in-the-loop interrupts mid-graph?

questions.question: How does the tool registry enforce safety for each call?
questions.answer: execute(name, args, ctx) looks up the ToolSpec; unknown tools raise ToolError. It checks role rank against spec.min_role (audit outcome 'denied' + Forbidden), checks requires_approval against ctx.approved_action_id (audit 'blocked' + ApprovalRequired 409), validates args with the input Pydantic model (ToolError on failure), runs the function, validates the output with the output model (audit 'error' + ToolError if invalid), and finally writes an audit event with args, side_effect and latency, returning the output plus a ToolCallRecord with a short summary. Both agents and the MCP server call this single function.
questions.reasoning: Tests the 'single choke point' pattern for agent tools.
follow_ups: Why validate tool outputs, not just inputs?
Which failures are not audited?

questions.question: Are denied or blocked tool calls always persisted in the audit log?
questions.answer: They are now, but originally they were not. execute() used to add the 'denied'/'blocked'/'error' AuditEvent to the caller's session and then raise; the caller's transaction is rolled back by that error (in _execute, in the HTTP handler, in the MCP handler), so the most security-relevant audit rows disappeared. The fix writes those events through audit_independent, which opens its own session and commits immediately, so they survive the caller's rollback. Successful calls still audit in the caller's transaction, which is correct: if the action rolls back, its success record should roll back too. Input-validation failures inside the tool are still not audited, a remaining gap. test_denied_tool_call_audit_survives_rollback reproduces the original bug.
questions.reasoning: Subtle transactional bug; tests whether the candidate understands when audit rows should and should not share the action's transaction.
follow_ups: Is it ever correct for audit rows to roll back with the action?
What is the cost of a second DB connection per denial?

questions.question: What does the MCP server expose and how is it secured?
questions.answer: mcp_server.py builds an MCPServer named nexus-ai over stdio. For each registry tool that is mcp_exposed, does not require approval and is not side_effect 'external', it generates a handler whose signature is synthesized from the tool's Pydantic input fields so the MCP SDK can publish a JSON schema. Each call opens a session, loads the service user from NEXUS_MCP_USER_EMAIL (default analyst@acme.example), rejects inactive/missing users, and runs the same registry execute(), so role checks, validation and audit apply; then it commits. send_email is never exposed (tested). draft_followup_email is exposed, so an MCP client can create pending approvals but not send.
questions.reasoning: Probes MCP knowledge and the principle of reusing the same authorization path for every entry point.
follow_ups: What are the risks of a single shared service user?
How would you add per-user auth to MCP?

questions.question: How do agents call tools and models, and how is that recorded?
questions.answer: Agents receive a StepContext. ctx.tool(name, **args) calls registry.execute with a ToolContext carrying the step's db, user and run_id, and appends {tool, args, ok, latency_ms, summary} to ctx.tool_calls. ctx.llm(request, schema, purpose) checks the token budget, calls get_llm().generate, records a usage_records row and appends an 'llm:<purpose>' entry to tool_calls. On step success the tool_calls list is stored on workflow_steps, which is what the RunDetail UI shows as agent activity.
questions.reasoning: Basic understanding of instrumentation around agent actions.
follow_ups: Why record tool calls on the step instead of only in audit?
What is lost when a step fails?

questions.question: Why does research_agent call customer_excerpt on document hits?
questions.answer: Shared documents like a delivery performance spreadsheet mention every customer in one chunk. Attaching whole chunks to each customer made the analysis infer false hypotheses (e.g. a 'delivery' problem for Northwind because Bluepeak's row was in the same chunk). customer_excerpt keeps only sentences/rows that mention the customer name (max 400 chars), and research keeps at most 3 such excerpts. test_shared_documents_do_not_create_false_hypotheses is the regression test. Limitation: name matching misses aliases or abbreviations.
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding of context contamination in agent pipelines, discovered by testing.
follow_ups: How would you handle customer aliases?
Could an attacker plant a customer name to inject text?

questions.question: How would you add a new tool with permission checks, for example create_crm_task?
questions.answer: Define input/output Pydantic models with bounds; implement fn(ctx, args) that scopes every lookup by ctx.user.org_id (404 on foreign ids); register a ToolSpec with min_role, side_effect='write' or 'external', and requires_approval=True if it touches an external system. If it has a real side effect, mirror the email pattern: a draft tool creates an ApprovalRequest with a deterministic idempotency key, and the approvals service executes it with approved_action_id. Decide mcp_exposed explicitly. Add tests for role denial, cross-tenant access, approval gating and idempotency. /tools in the admin API will list it automatically.
questions.reasoning: Practical extensibility question; checks the candidate applies all guard rails, not just the happy path.
follow_ups: Where would the approval executor branch on action type?
How do you keep the tool idempotent?

questions.question: How would you add a new agent that uses free-form tool calling (the model chooses tools), safely?
questions.answer: The current agents call tools in code; the model only plans, analyzes and drafts. For a tool-calling agent I would give the model only an allow-list of read tools (from REGISTRY filtered by side_effect='read' and the user's role), execute every call through registry.execute under the same StepContext, cap the number of tool calls and tokens per step (budget already exists), wrap tool outputs as untrusted data before returning them to the model, and keep side effects behind draft tools + approvals. Each loop iteration should be checkpointed or the whole loop treated as one idempotent step. Evaluate on fixed scenarios with failure injection before enabling.
questions.reasoning: Senior question on agent autonomy vs control; looks for allow-lists, budgets, untrusted output handling and approval gates.
follow_ups: How do you prevent tool-call loops?
How would you trace each tool decision?

questions.question: Explain the SQL behind get_top_customers and its trend calculation.
questions.answer: top_customers_with_trend computes end = as_of_date (latest order date for the org), mid = end - window months, start = mid - window months (months approximated as 30.44 days). It joins customers to orders within (start, end], groups by customer and uses conditional aggregates: SUM(CASE WHEN date > mid AND completed THEN amount) as recent, the same for <= mid as prior, and AVG of delivery delay per window. It orders by recent + prior DESC and limits to top_n. change_pct is computed in Python with Decimal ((r - p) / p * 100, 0 if p = 0).
questions.reasoning: SQL fluency: conditional aggregation, window boundaries and numeric precision.
follow_ups: Why are cancelled orders excluded from revenue but not from delay?
How would you do this with window functions?

questions.question: How is SQL injection prevented in the data layer?
questions.answer: All queries are built with SQLAlchemy Core/ORM expressions, so values are bound parameters, including LIKE patterns in search_customers and search_emails. The full-text query string is constructed only from [a-z0-9] tokens before being passed to to_tsquery. The only raw SQL is fixed statements (SELECT 1 in readyz, TRUNCATE built from model table names in the seed reset). Pydantic bounds limit input lengths and numbers for tools.
questions.reasoning: Basic security hygiene; follow-up often asks about LIKE wildcards and tsquery syntax.
follow_ups: Is a user-supplied '%' in LIKE a problem?
Where could ORDER BY injection happen?

questions.question: How is idempotency enforced at the database level?
questions.answer: approval_requests.idempotency_key and outbox_messages.idempotency_key have unique constraints (uq_approval_idem, uq_outbox_idem), and workflow_steps has a unique (run_id, name) constraint so a step cannot be duplicated per run. memory_items has unique (user_id, key) for upserts. Application code checks for an existing row first (draft tool, send tool), and the constraint is the backstop for races.
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding that check-then-insert needs a DB constraint behind it.
follow_ups: What error surfaces if two inserts race?
Would you use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT instead?

questions.question: How does claim_next avoid two workers taking the same job?
questions.answer: claim_next selects one job where status = 'queued' OR (status = 'processing' AND locked_at older than 10 minutes), ordered by created_at, LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Concurrent workers skip rows already locked by another transaction instead of blocking, so each gets a different job. The claim then sets status processing, locked_at = now, attempts += 1 and commits, releasing the row lock; from then on the status/locked_at columns, not the lock, represent ownership. The stale-lock clause reclaims jobs from crashed workers.
questions.reasoning: Classic Postgres queue question; candidates must explain SKIP LOCKED semantics and the lease model.
follow_ups: What happens to a job that legitimately runs longer than 10 minutes?
Is there an index that supports this query?

questions.question: What data is stored where, and what is not encrypted at the application layer?
questions.answer: Document bytes go to object storage under content-addressed keys '<org_id>/<sha256>.<ext>' (LocalStorage today); extracted chunk text and embeddings, emails, CRM/ERP rows, messages, approvals with email bodies, and audit details live in Postgres. Nothing is encrypted at the application layer; the threat model relies on disk/RDS/S3 encryption at rest. Also, deleting a document removes the row (chunks cascade) but the stored blob is not deleted - ObjectStorage has no delete method - which matters for data-retention and GDPR deletion requests.
questions.reasoning: Probes data lifecycle awareness, including a real gap in deletion.
follow_ups: How would you implement right-to-erasure end to end?
Should embeddings be considered personal data?

questions.question: How are migrations managed and how do tests get a clean database?
questions.answer: Alembic owns the schema (one initial revision creating all tables, HNSW and GIN indexes); env.py imports app.models so autogenerate sees all metadata and honors ALEMBIC_DATABASE_URL. The pgvector extension is created by an initdb script in Docker. Tests drop and recreate the public schema of a dedicated nexus_test database, create the vector extension, run alembic upgrade head and seed with the same seed script as the demo, once per session. Compose runs 'alembic upgrade head && python -m scripts.seed' before uvicorn in the api container.
questions.reasoning: Checks migration discipline and test isolation strategy.
follow_ups: Why not Base.metadata.create_all in tests?
How would you run migrations safely with multiple API replicas?

questions.question: How is multi-tenancy enforced?
questions.answer: It is application-level row scoping: every tenant-owned table has org_id, the JWT carries org, and current_user re-loads the user from the DB and rejects the token if the user's org_id differs from the claim. Every query then filters by user.org_id: retrieval filters both Chunk.org_id and Document.org_id, connectors take org_id explicitly, tools check fetched objects' org_id, and services raise NotFound for foreign ids. Tests cover documents, retrieval, runs and approvals across the acme and globex seeded tenants.
questions.reasoning: Foundational. Interviewers then probe what happens if one query forgets the filter.
follow_ups: What is your defense if a developer forgets a filter?
Would you use Postgres row-level security?

questions.question: Why return 404 rather than 403 for another tenant's resource?
questions.answer: A 403 confirms that the id exists and belongs to someone else, which leaks information (existence oracle) and helps enumeration. Returning the same NotFound as for a truly missing id makes foreign resources indistinguishable from nonexistent ones. The code does this consistently: get_document, get_run, approvals._load, conversations and memory, and tool lookups like _customer_orders. 403 is used only for role checks on the caller's own tenant (e.g. analyst approving). UUID ids make guessing hard anyway, but the policy does not rely on that.
questions.reasoning: A standard challenge question about information disclosure in authz responses.
follow_ups: Is there any endpoint where order of checks leaks existence?
How do you log these attempts for detection?

questions.question: A security researcher reports a cross-tenant data leak. How do you respond?
questions.answer: First contain: identify the endpoint/tool from the report and the audit log (audit_events has org_id, actor, action, target, request_id), disable the path if needed, and rotate JWT_SECRET only if token forgery is suspected. Reproduce with a test using the globex/acme fixtures. Likely root causes in this codebase are a query missing org_id (e.g. a new connector or a db.get without an org check) or a tool that trusts an id from model output. Fix with a scoped query and a regression test, then scan all db.get/select call sites for missing scoping. Determine blast radius from audit/request logs, notify affected tenants per policy, and consider defense in depth such as Postgres row-level security with a per-request app.org_id setting.
questions.reasoning: Incident-response maturity plus knowledge of where tenancy checks live in this code.
follow_ups: How would RLS interact with the worker and seed scripts?
What would you add to CI to catch this class of bug?

questions.question: How are JWTs issued and validated?
questions.answer: create_access_token signs HS256 tokens with sub (user id), org, role, iat, exp (ACCESS_TOKEN_MINUTES, default 60) and typ='access'. decode_access_token accepts only HS256, requires exp and sub, maps any PyJWTError to 401, and rejects typ != access. current_user then loads the user, checks is_active and that org matches. Authorization uses the DB role, not the role claim, so demotions apply immediately. Tests cover tampering, a token signed with another secret and alg=none.
questions.reasoning: JWT pitfalls: algorithm confusion, missing exp, stale claims.
follow_ups: Why include role in the token at all?
How would you revoke a token before expiry?

questions.question: The frontend keeps the JWT in sessionStorage. Defend or criticize that choice.
questions.answer: sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes and is not sent automatically, so there is no CSRF risk, and it is simple. But any script running in the page (XSS) can read it and exfiltrate the token for its 60-minute lifetime, and there are no refresh tokens or revocation. Mitigations present: React renders text nodes, the Markdown component never uses innerHTML (tested), and nginx sends a strict CSP (default-src 'self', connect-src 'self'). A stronger design is an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie session with CSRF protection, short access tokens and server-side revocation - listed as a known gap.
questions.reasoning: Common security trade-off question; the strong answer weighs XSS vs CSRF honestly.
follow_ups: What does connect-src 'self' buy you here?
How would you implement refresh tokens?

questions.question: How does URL ingestion defend against SSRF, and what gap remains?
questions.answer: fetch_url validates every hop: http/https only, no credentials in URL, host must match the URL_INGEST_ALLOWLIST (exact or subdomain), literal IPs rejected, DNS-resolved addresses must all be global and not multicast (blocks loopback, RFC1918, link-local such as 169.254.169.254, ULA IPv6). Redirects are followed manually (max 4 hops) and each Location is re-validated. Responses must be 200 with an allowed content type and are streamed with a byte cap; the client has a timeout. Gap: validate_url resolves DNS, then httpx resolves again to connect, so DNS rebinding (TOCTOU) can still reach an internal address. The documented production mitigation is an allowlisting egress proxy.
questions.reasoning: Very common security question. Must mention redirects, IPv6 and the rebinding gap.
follow_ups: How would you pin the resolved IP in httpx?
Why is the allowlist the most important control?

questions.question: How are uploaded files validated?
questions.answer: validate_upload rejects empty files and files over MAX_UPLOAD_MB (413), allows only pdf/docx/xlsx/csv/txt/md by extension, and never trusts the client Content-Type: PDFs must start with %PDF-; docx/xlsx must start with the ZIP magic, contain word/document.xml or xl/workbook.xml, contain no vbaProject.bin (macros), and pass a zip-bomb check (total uncompressed size over 200 MB or over 50x the archive size is rejected). Text types must not contain NUL bytes in the first 8 KB and must decode as UTF-8. Identical content per org (same sha256) is rejected with 409.
questions.reasoning: Tests layered file validation and why magic bytes beat MIME headers.
follow_ups: What about malicious PDFs targeting the parser?
Why reject non-UTF-8 text rather than guessing encodings?

questions.question: How is prompt injection from documents handled, and what are the limits of the regex scanner?
questions.answer: Defense in depth: at index time scan() runs six regex families (override_instructions, role_hijack, system_prompt_probe, fake_delimiters, exfiltration, tool_coercion) and stores hits in chunk.flags; flagged chunks stay searchable but are marked in the UI and API. All document and email text placed in prompts is wrapped by wrap_untrusted, which neutralizes a closing tag in the content, and system prompts say not to follow instructions inside those tags. Outputs are validated (citations, ground_sources), and side effects need human approval. The scanner itself is weak: paraphrases, other languages, encodings, or instructions split across chunks will pass, and it can false-positive on legitimate text. That is why it only flags and the real guarantees come from structural controls.
questions.reasoning: Challenge question: does the candidate rely on detection, or on architecture?
follow_ups: Why not drop flagged chunks from retrieval?
How would you evaluate injection robustness with a real model?

questions.question: The rate limiter is per process. What does that mean in practice and how would you fix it?
questions.answer: TokenBucketLimiter keeps buckets in a dict guarded by a lock, refilling at per_minute/60 tokens per second. Authenticated requests are keyed by user id plus the third path segment (so chat, documents, workflows have separate buckets); login is keyed by client IP with cost 6, about 10 attempts/min at the default 60/min. Being in-memory, limits multiply by the number of replicas and reset on restart, and buckets are never evicted. Behind nginx, request.client.host may be the proxy's address unless uvicorn trusts the proxy's forwarded headers, which would make all users share one login bucket. Fix: a Redis token bucket (atomic Lua script) keyed the same way, plus WAF rate rules at the edge.
questions.reasoning: Challenge about distributed state and correct client identification behind proxies.
follow_ups: Write the Lua script for a Redis token bucket.
How would you rate-limit per tenant as well as per user?

questions.question: How does login avoid user enumeration and brute force?
questions.answer: login rate-limits by IP before any DB work, looks the user up case-insensitively, and returns the same 401 'Invalid email or password' for an unknown user, an inactive user or a wrong password; denied attempts on existing users are audited. Passwords are argon2-hashed and verify_password returns False for malformed hashes. A timing side channel existed: unknown emails skipped argon2 verification, so fast responses revealed missing accounts. It was fixed by verifying the submitted password against a module-level dummy hash (_DUMMY_HASH) when the user does not exist, so both paths pay the argon2 cost. Remaining gaps: no account lockout, and behind a proxy the per-IP limiter sees the proxy IP unless uvicorn is told to trust forwarded headers.
questions.reasoning: Classic auth hardening plus the timing side channel; strong candidates know generic error messages alone are not enough.

questions.question: How does the system prevent an agent or an attacker from sending email without approval?
questions.answer: Multiple independent layers: send_email has requires_approval=True so registry.execute raises ApprovalRequired unless approved_action_id is set; only approvals.approve sets it, after _check_approver (manager+) and loading the request under SELECT FOR UPDATE scoped to the org; _send_email itself also refuses without approved_action_id; send_email has min_role manager and is excluded from MCP. Agents only call draft_followup_email. Approving twice returns the executed request without resending, and the outbox unique idempotency key blocks duplicates. Tests cover blocked sends, analyst denial, idempotent approval and the MCP exclusion.
questions.reasoning: Tests the layered-guard reasoning for high-impact actions.

questions.question: Would you add Postgres row-level security? How would it fit this codebase?
questions.answer: Today isolation depends on every query including org_id, which is one forgotten filter away from a leak. RLS would add a database-enforced backstop: enable RLS on tenant tables with a policy org_id = current_setting('app.org_id'), and set that GUC per transaction (SET LOCAL) from current_user in get_db, in run_step/_execute from the run's org, in the worker from the job's org and in the MCP handler from the service user. The app role must not be the table owner or must use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Complications: the worker's claim_next spans tenants (needs a separate role or policy), seed/migrations need a bypass role, connection pooling requires SET LOCAL not SET, and query plans should be checked. Not implemented.
questions.reasoning: Senior question on defense in depth and operational implications of RLS.

questions.answer: With the local LLM and hashing embedder, in-process: chat ask p50 37.9 ms, p95 52.1 ms (n=30) and a full investigation about 1.33 s p50 (n=3, max ~1.42 s). Chat time is mostly two Postgres queries (vector + full-text, 25 candidates each), Python reranking and persistence. The investigation is dominated by roughly 30 tool calls, per-step session/commit overhead and many approval inserts. questions.question: How is LLM cost tracked and controlled?
questions.answer: Every model call returns a Usage (provider, model, tokens, estimated cost, latency); estimate_cost uses PRICE_TABLE (USD per 1M tokens, marked as estimates) and the local adapter reports cost 0 with character-based token estimates. record_usage writes usage_records with purpose and run_id, aggregated in /admin/usage. Control: each run has token_budget (default 60k); StepContext.llm projects used + this step + prompt chars/4 before calling and raises BudgetExceeded, which ends the run as budget_exceeded. Model tiers (fast vs strong) let cheap calls use the fast model; only analysis uses 'strong'.

questions.question: What are the inaccuracies in the token budget enforcement?
questions.answer: The pre-call projection counts only the prompt (len(system + user) // 4), not expected output tokens, so a call can overshoot the budget. run.tokens_used is only incremented when a step commits, so tokens consumed by failed or timed-out attempts (and their usage_records, which are rolled back) are invisible to the budget and to cost reports. Retries can therefore spend real money untracked. Also the local adapter uses estimates. Fixes: reserve max_output tokens in the projection, write usage in a separate committed transaction, and charge failed attempts to the run.
questions.reasoning: Challenge question showing the candidate audits their own cost controls.
follow_ups: Where should a hard stop live: client or provider gateway?

questions.question: How is embedding done efficiently during ingestion?
questions.answer: index_document embeds chunk texts in batches of 64 (embedder.embed takes a list), adds Chunk rows, and commits once at the end in run_job, so a document is indexed atomically - existing chunks for the document are deleted in the same transaction, making re-indexing safe. Remote embedders send a batch per call with output dimensionality 384; Gemini vectors are re-normalized because truncated vectors are not unit length. There is no retry/backoff around remote embedding calls beyond the job-level retry (max 3 attempts).
questions.reasoning: Checks batching and transactional indexing.
follow_ups: What batch size would you use for OpenAI?

questions.question: Where are the likely performance bottlenecks as usage grows?
questions.answer: 1) Workflow execution in API BackgroundTasks and an 8-thread step pool shared by all runs in a process. 2) Python-side reranking that tokenizes every candidate text on each query (cheap at 50 candidates, but CPU per request). 3) Filtered HNSW recall/latency as chunks grow. 4) Polling: the UI polls run detail every 1.2 s and documents every 1.5 s, and workers poll the job table every 1 s. 5) A 10-connection pool per process with long-held sessions in steps. 6) Frontend bundle ~700 kB without code splitting. Each has a known remedy (run queue, caching, partitioning, SSE/LISTEN-NOTIFY, PgBouncer, code splitting).
questions.reasoning: Systems thinking about capacity; looks for specific bottlenecks rather than 'add caching'.

questions.question: How would you reduce LLM cost by an order of magnitude with a real provider?
questions.answer: Measure first from usage_records by purpose. Then: keep deterministic work deterministic (data_agent and report are already code); use the fast tier for planning and drafts (already) and test whether analysis can use fast with a stricter schema; trim prompts (cap excerpts, emails and quote lists - research already limits to 4 emails and 3 excerpts); cache plans for identical goals; batch the per-customer email drafts into one structured call returning a list; use provider prompt caching for the static system prompts; and lower retrieval k when rerank confidence is high. Guard each change with the EvalOps golden set. These are proposals; only tiers and limits exist today.
questions.reasoning: Senior cost-optimization reasoning tied to measurement and quality gates.

questions.question: Uploaded documents stay in 'pending' forever. How do you debug it?
questions.answer: Pending means the job was enqueued but no worker finished it. Check INGESTION_MODE: with 'worker' (as in docker-compose and tests) the API does not process jobs, so a worker process (python -m app.worker) must be running; locally, embedded mode starts a thread in the API. Then query ingestion_jobs for the document: status queued with attempts 0 means nobody is claiming; status queued with attempts > 0 and last_error set means it failed transiently and is being retried (doc status goes back to pending on retry); processing with an old locked_at means a worker died and the job will be reclaimed after 10 minutes. Worker logs (ingestion_failed with error_type) confirm.
questions.reasoning: Practical troubleshooting using the data model rather than guessing. The setup doc lists 'no worker' as the usual cause.
follow_ups: Which SQL would you run first?

questions.question: After a deploy, a workflow run shows 'running' forever. What happened and how do you recover?
questions.answer: execute_run runs inside the API process via BackgroundTasks, so if the process was killed mid-run nothing updates the row. On the next startup, lifespan calls mark_interrupted_runs, which marks a run 'interrupted' once it has shown no step activity for longer than stale_after_seconds(); a run that died moments before the restart is therefore picked up by a later restart, not immediately. A user (analyst+) can then POST /workflows/{id}/resume: resume_run resets non-completed steps to pending and execute_run reruns the graph, where completed steps are checkpoint hits. If a run stays 'running', check whether another replica is genuinely executing it (recent step timestamps) or whether startup recovery failed (startup_recovery_failed log).
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding of the crash-recovery path end to end, including the staleness rule.
follow_ups: Why can't you just resume a 'running' run?

questions.question: A PDF upload fails with 'No extractable text found'. Why, and will it be retried?
questions.answer: index_document raises EmptyDocument when chunking yields no drafts; for PDFs that typically means a scanned/image-only PDF since pypdf only extracts embedded text and there is no OCR. EmptyDocument subclasses ValueError, and run_job treats ValueError as non-retryable, so the job goes straight to failed and the document gets status failed with the error message - retrying would not help. The same applies to UnicodeDecodeError (a ValueError subclass). OCR support is a known limitation.
questions.reasoning: Checks knowledge of the retry classification and the OCR gap.
follow_ups: How would you add OCR without blocking the worker?
Is classifying all ValueErrors as permanent safe?

questions.question: All users suddenly get 429 on login in the containerized deployment, but not locally. Hypothesis?
questions.answer: The login limiter is keyed by request.client.host with cost 6 out of a 60-token bucket, about 10 attempts/min per key. Behind the nginx container, if uvicorn does not trust the proxy's X-Forwarded-For (uvicorn's --proxy-headers only honors trusted forwarded IPs, by default localhost), client.host is nginx's container IP, so every user shares one bucket and ten logins per minute exhaust it. Verify by logging client.host. Fix by configuring trusted proxy IPs (forwarded_allow_ips) or keying on a validated forwarded address, and longer term moving the limiter to Redis and the edge.
questions.reasoning: Debugging distributed/proxy behaviour; tests understanding of client identity behind proxies.
follow_ups: Why is trusting X-Forwarded-For blindly dangerous?

questions.question: A user says the assistant answers 'insufficient evidence' for a question clearly covered by a document. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: Use the response itself: the retrieval array shows which chunks were retrieved with vector_rank, keyword_rank, rerank_score and signals. If the right chunk is absent, check the document is status ready (retrieval filters ready only), belongs to the user's org, and whether the question's wording overlaps the chunk lexically - with the hashing embedder and full-text both lexical, paraphrases miss. If the chunk is present, the local answerer may have abstained because no single sentence covers 60% of the question terms. Reproduce with hybrid_search and the local _answer in a test; fixes range from rephrasing to a semantic embedder or query rewriting.
questions.reasoning: Tests a systematic retrieval-vs-generation diagnosis using built-in diagnostics.
follow_ups: How do you tell a retrieval miss from a generation miss in general?

questions.question: A run stays 'awaiting_approval' even though the manager approved everything. Why might that be?
questions.answer: A run moves to completed only via _maybe_complete_run, called after approve or reject, which completes the run when no approval for that run_id is still pending and the run status is awaiting_approval. So check for approvals still pending (some may be hidden by a UI filter), approvals created under a different run, or a run that was not in awaiting_approval at decision time (e.g. still running when the first approvals were decided - execute_run sets awaiting_approval only at the end). Also note approving an action other than send_email leaves it 'approved', which is not pending, so it would not block completion.

questions.question: An ingestion job for a very large document is processed twice concurrently. How is that possible?
questions.answer: claim_next reclaims 'processing' jobs whose locked_at is older than STALE_AFTER (10 minutes). The lock is a lease set once at claim time; there is no heartbeat. If indexing a huge document takes longer than 10 minutes, a second worker reclaims it while the first is still working. Both delete and re-insert the document's chunks in their own transactions, so the outcome is usually consistent (last commit wins) but work is duplicated and attempts are inflated toward max_attempts. Fix: a heartbeat that updates locked_at periodically, a lease token checked on completion, or a timeout bound on job duration.
questions.reasoning: Lease-based queues and the missing heartbeat; a classic distributed-systems pitfall.
follow_ups: How would you implement the heartbeat in a sync worker?
Could the two transactions deadlock?

Is the backend running on port 8101?'). HTTP errors with a response are different: they carry the server's code and request_id.
